# Misalignment of Low-Loss Regions Causes Grokking

Grokking refers to the delayed emergence of validation-set generalization after a model has already overfit the training set. Although first observed in small algorithmic tasks trained with transformers, its underlying mechanism remains unsettled. In this work, we develop an analysis framework based on mode connectivity and the geometry of low-loss regions. The framework predicts that the standard modular-arithmetic setting does not always produce grokking: under a symmetrypreserving train/validation split, we observe a stable anti-grokking case in which validation performance does not recover. This counterexample tests how several commonly discussed grokking indicators behave when grokking is absent.More broadly, our analysis framework and results further suggest that grokking arises when the low-loss regions induced by the training and validation partitions are misaligned. Once these regions become well aligned, training hyperparameters alone cannot produce grokking and the observed dynamics collapse to either trainable or non-trainable behavior.

Grokking is the phenomenon in which a neural network generalizes to a validation set only after a long period of apparent overfitting to the training set. It was first reported by OpenAI when training a two-layer transformer on modular arithmetic tasks (Power et al., 2022). This behavior contrasts with the usual expectation that training and validation accuracy improve on comparable timescales, and it has been discussed as a form of emergent generalization in which a model eventually discovers the structure underlying the data (Nanda et al., 2023; Wei et al., 2022). Prior work has approached grokking from several perspectives, including Fourier circuit (Nanda et al., 2023), representation learning (Liu et al., 2022), numerical stability (Prieto et al., 2025), Hessian geometry (Zhang et al., 2024), weight decay (Xu et al., 2026), the Slingshot effect (Thilak et al., 2022), and information leakage (Carvalho et al., 2025). These studies reveal useful patterns related to grokking, but they do not provide a full causal account of why grokking occurs. In this paper, we develop a geometric framework for analyzing grokking, based on empirical studies of Mode Connectivity (MC) (Draxler et al., 2018; Tian et al., 2025). Singular Learning Theory (SLT)

suggests that Low-Loss Regions (LLRs)1 in neural-network parameter spaces are better understood as extended valleys than as isolated basins (Li et al., 2018; Ainsworth et al., 2023; Lion et al., 2024). MC provides empirical tools for identifying low-loss paths between independently trained minima. Our analysis framework predicts that the OpenAI modular-arithmetic setting does not necessarily produce grokking. We validate this prediction by constructing an anti-grokking split that reliably prevents delayed validation improvement while leaving the model architecture, optimizer, dataset size, and task family unchanged. We then use this case to examine whether commonly discussed indicators also occur when grokking is absent. Several indicators do not by themselves predict this absence, suggesting that they should be interpreted as correlates rather than complete causal

Our analysis suggests that grokking requires two ingredients. First, the low-loss regions defined by the training and validation partitions must be sufficiently misaligned. Second, the training trajectory must enter the overlap of these regions in a delayed manner, a condition shaped by hyperparameters such as learning rate and weight decay. We regard the first ingredient as the root cause because grokking does not occur when these low-loss regions are well aligned, whereas the second ingredient controls how training moves through the low-loss regions. In practical terms, low-loss regions are easier to misalign when the information carried by the training partition is small relative to the expressive capacity of the model. This paper makes the following contributions: 1. We provide a geometric analysis framework that accounts for several proposed causes of grokking through the misalignment of low-loss regions. 2. Based on this framework, we identify counterexamples within the OpenAI grokking setup that do not exhibit grokking. These anti-grokking cases show that several commonly used indicators are not sufficient on their own to predict grokking. 3. Based on this framework, we show that low-loss regions shrink and become more aligned as the information carried by the training partition increases. When the low-loss regions are fully aligned, grokking cannot occur. The paper is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the terminology and reviews prior work on grokking and mode connectivity. Section 3 presents our low-loss-region framework and the antigrokking example, showing that grokking does not always occur in the OpenAI grokking setup. Section 4 studies the alignment of low-loss regions. Section 5 discusses the implications of these results, and Section 6 concludes the paper. 2 TERMINOLOGY AND EXISTING WORK This section introduces the terminology used throughout the paper, reviews the OpenAI modulararithmetic setup that we reuse in our experiments, summarizes several influential grokking explanations, and then describes mode connectivity, which is the empirical starting point for our framework.

Consider a model architecture M with d trainable parameters, a fixed dataset D, and a loss function L. Each parameter vector P ∈ Rd induces a loss value on D. For a threshold Lth, we define the corresponding low-loss region SL≤Lth as SL≤Lth := {P ∈ Rd | L(P, D) ≤ Lth} (1) This region is determined by the model architecture M, dataset D, loss function L, and threshold Lth. It is independent from the optimizer and training hyperparameters. In principle, evaluating the loss at every point in parameter space would determine the boundary of this region. We therefore write Equation 1 as the following mapping: SL≤Lth = LLR(M, D, L, Lth) (2) 1The sets of model weights whose loss is below a specified threshold.

where LLR stands for Low-Loss Region. Since the loss function is coupled with the architecture and the threshold is adjusted to select a contour level, we use the concise notation SL≤Lth = LLR(M, D) when these choices are clear from context. We use the following notation for the overlap of the low-loss regions induced by two datasets2: LLR(M, D1 + D2) := {P ∈ Rd | P ∈ LLR(M, D1) ∧ P ∈ LLR(M, D2)} Similarly, we define the part of LLR(M, D1) that does not overlap with LLR(M, D2) as LLR(M, D1+!D2) := {P ∈ Rd | P ∈ LLR(M, D1) ∧ P /∈ LLR(M, D2)} 2.2 SET UP GROKKING EXPERIMENTS Grokking was first observed when training a simple transformer on a modular arithmetic dataset (Power et al., 2022). We reuse this experimental setup and denote the corresponding model architecture by Mgrok. The full architecture and training recipe are provided in Appendix A. The modular arithmetic dataset maps integer pairs (x, y) to f (x, y) mod m, where m is the modulus and x, y ∈ {0, . . . , m − 1}. We write this dataset as Dmod(f (x, y), m). Modular addition is the most commonly studied function in grokking research (Nanda et al., 2023; Thilak et al., 2022). We illustrate Dmod(x + y, 10) in Figure 1(a). The original OpenAI setup uses Dmod(x + y, 97) with randomly 50% of the samples assigned to training and the remainder assigned to validation (Power et al., 2022). We follow this setup and reproduce grokking3, see Figure 1(b).

2.3 EXISTING WORK ON GROKKING Prior work has proposed several mechanisms and empirical indicators associated with grokking. We summarize the main indicator claims most relevant to our analysis below. 1. Slingshot effect Thilak et al. (Thilak et al., 2022) report that grokking almost exclusively occurs near the onset of Slingshots and is absent in runs without them. Prior work suggests that the formation of this Fourier circuit can be used as a progress measure for grokking (Nanda et al., 2023). 2.4 EXISTING WORK ON MODE CONNECTIVITY Mode connectivity is the empirical observation that two independently trained models can be connected by a low-loss path (Draxler et al., 2018). This property has been observed for ResNet (He et al., 2015), VGG (Simonyan & Zisserman, 2015), and DenseNet (Huang et al., 2018) models trained on CIFAR-10. More recently, the Low-Loss Path Finding (LLPF) method extended this observation to transformer architectures (Tian et al., 2025). We empirically validate mode connectivity for Mgrok on Dmod(x + y, 97) using LLPF. Configuration details and results are provided in Appendix B. For two independently trained Mgrok models, the maximum loss along the discovered path remains below 1.5 × 10−3 and the minimum accuracy remains above 99.85%. Repeating this experiment ten times yields only small standard deviation across runs. These empirical results motivate Conjecture 1. Conjecture 1. The low-loss region LLR(Mgrok, Dmod(x + y, 97), L, 1.5 × 10−3) is a single pathconnected region. This conjecture is consistent with the LLPF interpretation that repeated success across different pairs of modes trained on random seeds provides evidence for a path-connected low-loss region. The “path” should be understood as evidence of a higher-dimensional connected manifold rather than a literal one-dimensional structure: LLPF identifies one-dimensional curves, but the underlying connected set is expected to have dimension greater than one (Benton et al., 2021). There is also theoretical support for this perspective, please see Appendix O. We also clarify that MC should not be conflated with linear mode connectivity, see Appendix P.

3 ANALYSIS FRAMEWORK AND ANTI-GROKKING EXAMPLE This section introduces our analysis framework and uses it to identify a corner case in the OpenAI modular-arithmetic setup where grokking does not occur. We call this behavior anti-grokking. We then use the anti-grokking case to test whether several existing grokking indicators can predict the

Consider a dataset D split into a training partition Dtrain and a validation partition Dval. These two partitions induce two low-loss regions, LLR(M, Dtrain) and LLR(M, Dval). Because Dtrain ̸= Dval, the corresponding low-loss regions are not completely identical. In the grokking experiment shown in Figure 1(b), the training partition is randomly sampled from Dmod(x + y, 97) and contains 50% of the whole dataset. We therefore expect the two induced low-loss regions to have a comparable volume: V (LLR(M, Dtrain)) ≈ V (LLR(M, Dval)). When the two regions are comparable in volume but not identical, some weight vectors P may lie in LLR(M, Dtrain) without lying in LLR(M, Dval). We call this set the non-overlap low-loss region and write the non-empty condition as

For Mgrok and Dmod(x + y, 97), this overlap is not empty because Figure 1(b) shows that some parameter vectors achieve low loss on both training and validation partitions. In other settings, however, the overlap may be empty, for example when the architecture is inappropriate for the task or when the labels are randomly generated. Combining Conjecture 1 with Equations 3 and 4 yields the geometric illustration in Figure 3. This illustration is schematic and does not encode dimensionality 4.

Figure 3: Geometric illustration of LLR(Mgrok, Dmod(x + y, 97)) in the weight space. Motivated by Conjecture 1, we draw connected paths representing LLR(Dtrain) and LLR(Dval). Equations 3 and 4 indicate that both overlap and non-overlap regions exist for the grokking setup, so the two low-loss regions are not aligned. The four learning trajectories (Comprehension, Grokking, Memorization, and Confusion) correspond to the learning phases identified in (Liu et al., 2022). Existing grokking work identifies four learning phases (Liu et al., 2022): • Comprehension: accuracy on Dtrain and Dval increases at approximately the same time. • Grokking: validation accuracy increases much later than training accuracy. 4For example, point A should not be interpreted as a zero-dimensional point in Rd, and curve ⌢ AB should not be interpreted as a literal one-dimensional curve. Likewise, the figure does not imply that exactly one LLR(Dtrain) path intersects exactly one LLR(Dval) path. Several high-dimensional branches may intersect in the overlap region.

• Memorization: only training accuracy increases. • Confusion: neither training nor validation accuracy increases. These trajectories are also shown in Figure 3. Because the illustration is dimension-free, it should not be read as implying that comprehension is less likely than other phases merely because the drawn trajectory appears to pass through a point. The grokking trajectory in Figure 3 has two stages: (1) entering LLR(Dtrain) and (2) moving from LLR(Dtrain) into LLR(Dtrain + Dval). The first stage is the ordinary outcome of minimizing training loss, whereas the second requires explaining why optimization continues after training accuracy has saturated and why that continued motion can reach the overlap region. Appendix J gives a lossbased explanation: correctly classified training examples can still have nonzero cross-entropy, so the training loss can keep decreasing after training accuracy reaches 100%. This continued optimization can move the parameters through the training-only region and into the overlap when that region is accessible. Since low-loss regions are determined by M and D, modifying the train/validation split can therefore alter whether this transition is possible.

Based on our analysis framework and prior discussion, we find one way to prevent the second stage using the notion of surprisal from Shannon information theory (Shannon, 1948). Each sample in a binary modular arithmetic dataset maps two variables a and b to an output c. For Dmod(x + y, 97), the function f (x, y) = x + y satisfies the symmetry f (a, b) = f (b, a). We treat this symmetry as task knowledge. If the fact f (a, b) = c is known together with this symmetry, then observing f (b, a) = c should have lower surprisal than it would without the symmetry. This suggests that a train/validation split can preserve the same training ratio while reducing the effective surprisal of the training partition. Empirically, we find such a corner case: grokking is eliminated by enforcing this symmetry in the partition. We call this the anti-grokking example. We randomly generate a train/validation partition for Dmod(x + y, 97) such that paired samples f (a, b) and f (b, a) always belong to the same partition, as shown in Figure 4(a). Training Mgrok with the same hyperparameters on this anti-grokking split does not produce grokking, as shown in Figure 4(b). The only change relative to Figure 1(b) is the train/validation split.

Figure 4: Anti-grokking setup. (a) Dataset partition for the anti-grokking example on Dmod(x + y, 97). Unlike a random partition, samples located at (a, b) and (b, a) always belong to the same partition. The numbers 4705 and 4704 indicate the sample counts in the two partitions. (b) Training Mgrok with the same hyperparameters on the split shown in Figure 4(a) does not produce grokking: validation accuracy remains low, and validation loss does not decrease. Section 2 summarized three indicators often associated with grokking: (1) the Slingshot effect, (2) the Fourier-based generalization circuit, and (3) a critical training-set size. We revisit these indicators in the anti-grokking example to examine whether they are also sufficient to guarantee

In the anti-grokking example, Slingshot spikes are still observed, see Figure 5(a). Thilak et al.’s Figure 5 already shows that Slingshot effects and grokking can separate across datasets and training configurations, including cases with Slingshot effects but no grokking (Thilak et al., 2022). Our experiment provides a complementary observation: this relationship can also change within the same task, model, optimizer, and complete dataset when only the train/validation split is changed. Thus, our experiment shows that a Slingshot is not sufficient by itself to guarantee grokking.The Fourier component plot in Figure 5(b) also shows that some frequencies have larger components than others, although the concentration is much weaker than in Figure 2(b). However, using this signal as a progress measure is misleading in this case: Figure 4(b) shows no progress toward grokking, whereas the Fourier components suggest slight progress.

Figure 5: Anti-grokking diagnostics. (a) A Slingshot pattern similar to Figure 2(a) is observed in the anti-grokking example. Thus, the Slingshot effect is not by itself a faithful explanation of grokking. (b) Compared with Figure 2(b), several frequencies still have larger components than others, but the concentration is much weaker than in the grokking case. The claim that the training set must exceed a size threshold is also incomplete, because the antigrokking example keeps the training-set size fixed. A more precise statement is that grokking requires the training partition to carry sufficient effective information to recover the task. This effective information entropy is not determined solely by the raw number of samples: it should account for task knowledge that makes some samples informative about others. Appendix I.1 operationalizes this idea for the symmetry f (a, b) = f (b, a) and shows that symmetry-aware training coverage provides a useful empirical proxy for effective information entropy. Prior work has used entropy-based notions for datasets (Shi et al., 2025; Schwalbe-Koda et al., 2025; Zhang et al., 2020), but has not explicitly incorporated task knowledge in this way. A formal entropy measure that incorporates task knowledge is left for future work. Finally, the requirement that samples at (a, b) and (b, a) appear in the same partition is not an all-or-nothing condition. In the anti-grokking split, 100% of such pairs share a partition. As this ratio is reduced toward 70%, grokking gradually reappears, see Appendix I. 4 ALIGNMENT OF LOW-LOSS REGIONS This section analyzes how low-loss regions change as the dataset becomes larger. We first argue that adding data imposes additional constraints and therefore tends to shrink low-loss regions. We then empirically show that, as these regions shrink, the train and validation low-loss regions become increasingly aligned. Under such alignment, grokking disappears and training dynamics collapse to either trainable or non-trainable. 4.1 SHRINKING OF LOW-LOSS REGION The volume of a low-loss region should decrease, or at least not increase, as the dataset grows. When one dataset is a subset of another, this monotonic relation can be written as

loss on D1 also satisfies the constraints imposed by D2. This intuition is consistent with empirical work showing that models typically incur higher loss on additional out-of-distribution data than on in-distribution data (Zhang et al., 2017; Salman & Liu, 2019). However, with average loss, this relationship should be understood as a geometric heuristic rather than a strict theorem, because errors on different samples can compensate for one another. We slightly modify the modular-dataset construction so that it satisfies the nested-dataset condition in Equation 5. We first generate a single master dataset Dmod1997(xy , 1997), and use the same tokenizer for all derived datasets. For each n ≤ 1997, we then define Dmod1997(f, n) by retaining only those samples whose operands satisfy x, y ∈ {0, . . . , n − 1}. The targets remain f (x, y) mod 1997 for every n; thus, n indexes the operand-domain size rather than the modulus. Consequently, for any m < n, Dmod1997(f, m) ⊆ Dmod1997(f, n). Increasing n therefore adds labeled examples and imposes additional constraints. Accordingly, Equation 5 suggests that the volume V (LLR(Mgrok, Dmod1997(f, n))) should be non-increasing as n grows. 4.2 ALIGNMENT OF LOW-LOSS REGIONS The grokking setup has two low-loss regions, LLR(Mgrok, Dmod1997,train(f, n)) and LLR(Mgrok, Dmod1997,val(f, n)). As n increases, both regions shrink. The key question is how the overlap region, LLR(M, Dtrain + Dval), and the non-overlap region, LLR(M, Dtrain+!Dval), change during this shrinkage. Our analysis is that the overlap region should shrink but would never become an empty set as long as the task remains learnable. Otherwise, no model could fit both the training and validation partitions. By contrast, the non-overlap region should decrease as the two low-loss regions shrink. This process is illustrated in Figure 6.

Figure 6: Low-loss regions defined by the training and validation partitions become increasingly aligned as partition size increases. The overlap region is illustrated as a connected path because mode connectivity is empirically verified to persist for LLR(Mgrok, Dtrain + Dval) in Appendix B. To test this analysis, we design an empirical experiment that indirectly probes the overlap region, as shown in Figure 7. The procedure is inspired by prior work studying the effect of training hyperparameters on grokking (Liu et al., 2022). Specifically, we sweep learning rate and weight decay, train on Dmod1997(xy , n), and classify the resulting learning phase for each hyperparameter pair5. We then count how many cells belong to each learning phase as n increases. A decrease in Memorization cells together with an increase in Comprehension cells suggests that fewer trajectories terminate in the training-only low-loss region and more trajectories directly reach the overlap of LLR(Dtrain) and LLR(Dval). A complete explanation of why phase-cell counts provide an indirect probe of low-loss-region alignment is given in Appendix C. We perform these experiments on Dmod1997(xy , n) for n ∈ {97, 197, 297, 397, 597, 797, 1997} and the results are shown in Figure 7. The four learning phases follow Figure 3, and the empirical classification criteria are given in Appendix D. This experiment is not a direct measurement of low-loss-region volume. Precisely measuring such a volume is computationally infeasible because it would require exploring a high-dimensional parameter space. The phase diagrams in Figure 7 should therefore be interpreted as an approximate probe based on sweeping weight decay and learning rate. As a complementary diagnostic, Appendix K applies a symmetric train/validation measurement to the same nested modular-dataset family to provide an approximate quantification of the misalignment level. 5Our setup is close to Figure 6 of (Liu et al., 2022).
